before.author: Folio editorial

content.text: Your client has approved the work. The files are delivered, the revisions are finished, and one task remains: sending the invoice.

That should be straightforward. But a blank document brings up several questions. What belongs on it? How should you show a deposit? Do you need a separate line for every task? And how do you make the finished invoice look organized?
A free invoice generator handles the layout and calculations while you supply the details. Enter your business and customer information, describe the work, check the amounts, and download a PDF.
The most useful invoice is one your client can understand without asking you to explain it. Here’s how to create one.
Gather your details before opening the editor
Start with the information you already agreed on with your client: the work completed, its price, payment timing, and any deposit received.
Keep these details nearby:
Your business or trading name and contact information.
The customer’s billing name and address.
An invoice number.
The issue date and agreed due date.
Descriptions of the goods or services.
Quantities, rates, and the agreed currency.
Applicable adjustments and payment instructions.
Ask your client whether they need a purchase order number or a specific project reference. Including it from the beginning can save an extra round of emails.
Use a consistent invoice numbering system, such as
. The practical goal is to make each invoice easy to identify when someone mentions it later.
Create your invoice step by step
Folio’s
free invoice generator
provides a live preview, customizable designs, and PDF downloads without a Folio watermark. You can begin without an account.
1. Enter the business and customer information
Open the invoice editor and fill in both sides of the transaction.
Use the customer’s billing details rather than assuming their project contact’s name is sufficient. A freelancer may invoice a company even when all communication happens with one employee.
Check your own contact information, too. A client should be able to reach you if they have a question about a charge.
2. Set the invoice number, dates, and currency
Give the invoice its unique reference and enter the relevant dates.
An explicit due date is easier to act on than a vague request to pay “soon.” Use the payment timing already agreed with your customer.
Check the currency before entering prices. Selecting a different currency changes how amounts are presented; Folio does not automatically convert your rates using an exchange rate.
3. Describe the work clearly
A line labeled “Services” tells the customer very little.
“Homepage copywriting — five sections, including one revision” gives them something they can connect to the project.
For hourly work, enter the hours as the quantity and your hourly price as the rate. For a fixed project fee, a quantity of one usually makes the calculation straightforward.
You don’t need to reproduce your entire timesheet. Include enough detail to explain the charge and distinguish it from other work.
4. Add adjustments and payments already received
Enter any agreed discount, relevant shipping charge, or applicable tax settings.
Keep a deposit separate from a discount. A discount reduces the price; a deposit records money the customer has already paid.
Folio provides an
Amount already paid
field for that purpose. Enter only payments you have actually received, then check the remaining balance.
The generator applies the figures and settings you supply. It does not determine which tax rules apply to your transaction.

Imagine a fictional design project with these charges, in USD:
Description
Quantity
Rate
Amount
Logo design
4 hours
Business card layout
Subtotal
Agreed discount
Total
Deposit already received
Balance due
This example leaves out tax and shipping to keep the arithmetic clear.
The distinction between the total and the balance matters. The project costs $400 after the discount, but the client only needs to pay another $300.

Once the amount is correct, explain how to pay it.
For a bank transfer, provide the relevant payment details and a useful reference, such as the invoice number. Check every character before sending.

Payment features and limits
Test the link yourself. Confirm that it opens the intended destination and belongs to the correct recipient.
Choose a design that makes the invoice easy to scan
A logo and a brand color can help a customer recognize your business. They should also leave the important information easy to find.

Who issued the invoice.
What the customer is being charged for.
When payment is due.
How much remains to be paid.
Long descriptions deserve particular attention. A useful explanation becomes harder to read if it crowds the quantity or amount columns.
Choose the paper size you intend to use, then inspect the whole document. Folio offers A4 and US Letter output, and longer invoices can continue onto additional pages.
Keep an editable copy as well as the PDF
The PDF is the document you send. An editable draft is what you’ll want if the client requests a corrected address or an additional reference.

Save to account
stores the invoice in your private library. The
privacy policy
explains these differences.

INV-2026-014-CustomerName.pdf

Start with the work you’ve already agreed on
You don’t need an elaborate billing document for a straightforward job. You need accurate details, understandable charges, and a clear next step for the customer.
Open the
invoice generator at
thebestfreepdf.com
, enter one real or practice project, and review the preview as though you were receiving it. Before closing the editor, keep both the finished PDF and an editable draft.

Can I create an invoice on my phone?
Yes. Folio supports mobile editing and previewing. After generating the PDF, use the available download or share action, then check your browser’s downloads or Files app.
Mobile instructions

Folio supports up to 50 line items per invoice. Signed-in users can also explicitly save up to 200 invoices in their account for free.

before.title: Free PDF Editor: Add Text, Fill Forms, and Sign a PDF
before.author: Folio Editorial

content.text: You have a PDF to complete, a few blank spaces to fill, and no reason to print it. A free PDF editor can handle that kind of work: add your answers, mark an instruction, place a visual signature, and download the completed document.

Adding information to a page is different from rewriting words already in the PDF, and both workflows are free in Folio. You can download additions, annotations, visual signatures, forms, and original-text changes without payment. Every account includes 1 GB of private storage. This guide helps you choose the right editing tool for the task.
What can you do with a free PDF editor?
Task
How to handle it in Folio
Free finished PDF?
Write a name or answer in a blank space
Add Text
Yes.
Complete supported interactive fields
Fill existing fields
Yes.
Highlight, draw, or add a comment
Annotation tools
Yes.
Place a drawn, typed, or uploaded visual signature
Sign
Yes.
Add text fields or checkboxes to a form
Form tools
Yes.
Replace words that were already in the document
Edit Text
Yes, including original-text changes.

Free exports do not receive a Folio watermark. File and storage limits still apply, so free access should not be read as unlimited capacity. The main editor accepts a PDF up to 50 MB; some other operations have smaller limits.
A quick workflow for a document with blank spaces
Open the
free PDF editor
, choose your file, and wait for its preview. Keep a separate original so you can start again if you need to. For a simple registration form, the following sequence is usually enough.
Read the entire form before filling the first box. Check which sections you are supposed to complete.
Use existing form fields when the PDF provides them. For a blank printed line without a field, choose Add Text.
Place the answer in the empty area and enter your information. Adjust size and position so the answer fits without covering the question.
Add a signature only if the document requires one and the recipient accepts that signing method.
Review all pages, including any checkboxes, dates, and instructions at the end.
Choose Download PDF, save the result, and open that saved copy to verify it before sending.
Add text so it looks like it belongs on the page

Select Add Text and place the text box where the answer should go. Use a readable size that suits the nearby labels. On a form with ruled lines, align the answer above the line rather than through it. A little space at both ends is more useful than squeezing a long answer against the box edges.

Suppose a workshop form asks for “Organization” on a short line. “Northside Community Workshop” may not fit at the default size. Reduce the size modestly or use an allowed second line; do not cover the next question. If the instructions require a full registered name, do not shorten it simply to make the layout easier.

Review the page at a normal reading size after positioning the box. A label can look tidy while zoomed in and still be too small to read when the full page is visible. Use Undo if a change makes the placement worse, and adjust the added text box while it is still in your workspace.
Use the form fields when they are available

An interactive field stores an answer in a defined place. A drawn rectangle or printed line only looks like a field. If you cannot enter information directly into the PDF’s existing controls, check whether the page is a flat form before assuming the editor has failed.

In Folio, open More tools and choose Fill existing fields to work with supported fields in the Form panel. Fill the relevant text entries, checkboxes, or available choices there. For a flat form that does not offer those controls, Add Text can place a visible answer in an empty area.
If you are creating a reusable form for other people, use
Create a PDF form
to add text fields and checkboxes. Give them clear, distinct names. The
W3C’s PDF form guidance
explains why field names and control information matter to assistive technology. Adding fields alone is not a complete accessibility check.
Decide whether the recipient should still be able to fill the fields

Leave Flatten fields when exporting off if someone still needs to complete the form. If you need a completed copy whose fields are no longer interactive, that option can be useful. Keep an unflattened original before using it.

Flattening fields is not document security. It does not prevent every kind of later editing, remove hidden information, or verify who completed the form. Choose it for how the fields should behave, not as a substitute for a separate protection or signing process.
Place a signature without turning the whole page into a photo

Choose Sign to draw a signature, or use its menu to type one or upload a signature image. Select Add signature, then position and resize it in the intended space. Keep it clear of printed text, and add the date separately when the form asks for it.

A drawn signature does not need to be large to remain clear. If you are working with a finger on a phone, create the shape at a comfortable size first, then reduce it on the page. Inspect thin strokes after resizing so the result remains readable.
For a signature image to use elsewhere, the separate
signature generator

exports a transparent PNG. Inserting that PNG into a PDF and downloading the PDF is a separate step. A placed image is a visual signature; it does not add identity verification, a signing audit trail, or a digital certificate. Follow the recipient’s signing instructions.
Avoid two common shortcuts that cause problems
Typing over an existing sentence

If the address already printed on a document is wrong, placing a new text box on top does not reliably replace it. Old characters can remain visible around the new ones, and the old information may still exist beneath a cover. Use original-text editing when supported, or correct the source document and export a fresh PDF.

Use Add Text for a new note or answer and Edit Text for a correction to supported original words. Both are free to use and download. If a change does not look right, undo it, adjust it, and check the finished PDF.
Treating an eraser or white box as secure redaction

Removing something you added in the current editing session is different from permanently removing content already stored in a PDF. Folio’s visual covering tools should not be used to hide information that must be deleted securely. Use a dedicated redaction workflow when permanent removal is the requirement, and verify the resulting document.
Understand where the working PDF is saved

Folio’s main editor uploads the opened PDF and saves the workspace privately for recovery. Guest workspaces expire after 24 hours. This is separate from the free annotation processing that runs in your browser, and separate again from a copy downloaded to your device.
Check
Folio’s privacy page

before opening a document that has specific storage requirements. The editor’s All changes saved message refers to the workspace; it does not mean a finished PDF has been saved in your device’s file manager. Use Download PDF for that copy.
Download and verify the completed document

On a phone, Folio can show a Your file is ready dialog after preparing the export. Choose Download file, or Share file when available, and complete the save action offered by your device. If a PDF preview opens, use its Save or Share control. The
phone editing guide
explains the iPhone and Android file locations.
Open the downloaded PDF outside the editing workspace.
Read every answer and check whether it is clipped or overlaps a label.
Confirm that checkboxes and signatures appear on the intended pages.
Test whether fields remain interactive if the recipient needs to fill them.
Give the completed file a recognizable name and attach that copy.
Questions about using a free PDF editor
Can I edit a scanned PDF for free?

You can add text, highlights, and a visual signature over a readable scan. Replacing the words inside the scanned image requires a different process, usually OCR followed by editing. Folio does not include standalone OCR, so a scanned paragraph does not become editable original text just because you open it.
Will my PDF look exactly the same after editing?

Your additions should be checked in the saved result. Different document structures, fonts, and PDF viewers can affect what you see. A short sample edit and download is a useful first check before completing a long form. Keep the source until the final copy has been accepted.
What if I need to rewrite several paragraphs?

Ask for the original editable document if it is available. A word processor can move paragraphs and adjust page flow more naturally than editing separate text objects inside a PDF. For a small supported correction in Folio, use Edit Text and review the
text editor’s capabilities
before relying on that export.
For a form entry, note, or visual signature, you can keep the task simple:
open the free PDF editor
, make the addition, and inspect the downloaded copy. You should leave with a document that is complete and easy for its next reader to use.

Kelly Sikkema
on Unsplash.

before.title: How to Create, Fill, and Sign a PDF Form
before.author: Folio Editorial

content.text: A useful form makes the next action obvious. The reader knows what to enter, where to enter it, and what to do with the completed document. Whether you are preparing an event registration sheet or completing a project checklist, a few thoughtful field choices can remove unnecessary back-and-forth.

Folio supports two common workflows: filling supported fields that already exist in a PDF, and adding text fields or checkboxes to a PDF background. You can also place a visual signature on the page. Start by deciding whether you are creating a reusable form or finishing a single copy.
Check whether the PDF already has fields

Open the document through Fill & sign. Supported text fields, checkboxes, dropdowns, and radio groups appear in the workspace’s Form panel. Use these existing fields when they are available; they connect your answer to the form’s intended structure.

A printed line or an empty box is not necessarily an interactive field. If the Form panel has no usable fields, the PDF may be a flat page or a scan. You can add text annotations to complete your own copy, or create real fields if other people will need to fill the document later.
Build a reusable form
Open Create a PDF form and choose the PDF that will provide the page layout.
Choose Text field from More tools and place a field beside the relevant question or label.
Give the field a meaningful, unique name in its properties. For example, use participant_name and contact_email for separate answers.
Choose Checkbox for a simple yes-or-no response or an individual item in a checklist.
Adjust field positions and sizes, then mark fields as required where that matches the intended workflow.
Leave reusable fields empty and export without flattening so recipients can enter their own answers.

A field’s internal name and its visible question do different jobs. “contact_email” is a useful internal name, but the reader still needs a clear label such as “Email address” printed beside the box. Keep instructions close to the field rather than forcing readers to search the top of the page.
Design fields for the answers you expect

Leave enough width for realistic names and addresses. A narrow box may look tidy when it is empty but become difficult to use when someone enters a longer response. Checkboxes need enough surrounding space that their purpose is unambiguous, especially when several choices appear on the same line.

For an event form, a simple structure might include participant name, contact email, organization, and a checkbox for a specific attendance option. Avoid asking for information you do not need. Fewer, clearer questions make the completed form easier to review.

The current form builder creates text fields and checkboxes. It can fill supported existing dropdowns and radio groups, but those additional field types are not part of its current creation tools. Plan your layout around the controls you can actually provide.
Fill the form and add a visual signature

Use the Form panel to enter values and review your answers against the page. For a non-interactive area, Add Text can place information directly on the document. Choose Sign for a typed signature, or use Pencil to draw a signature by hand. Position it within the intended signature area and check that it does not cover a date or printed name.

Folio adds a visual signature. It does not provide a certificate-based digital signature, identity verification, or a signing audit trail. Check what format the recipient requires before completing the document.
Choose an interactive or flattened export

Keep fields interactive when the next person must enter or change answers. This is the appropriate choice for a blank master that you plan to reuse. Flatten fields when exporting turns their current appearances into page content, so the exported fields can no longer be filled.

Flattening is useful for a finished reading copy, but it is not a guarantee that the entire PDF can never be edited. Keep a separate interactive master if you may need to revise answers or issue the form again. Give the two files distinct names so you do not accidentally send an empty master instead of a completed copy.
Test the form before sending it out

Open the exported form in the PDF reader your recipients are likely to use. Enter a long sample answer, check the boxes, save, and reopen the file to confirm the values remain visible. Field appearance and behavior can vary between readers, so this small test is more useful than judging only the editor preview.

for a reusable template, or
Fill & sign
to complete a document you have received.

before.author: Folio editorial

content.text: You open the PDF, click the sentence, and nothing happens.
To edit original text in a PDF, you need an editor that can select and replace the document’s existing text blocks. In Folio, the editor at
thebestfreepdf.com
, that means opening your document and choosing
Edit Text
. Supported text can then be changed directly on the page.
Before you start, though, check what kind of PDF you have. That small step can save you a lot of clicking.
First, check whether the words are actually text
Try selecting a few words in your PDF viewer and copying them into a blank document.
If recognizable text appears, your PDF likely contains a text layer. That gives an original-text editor something to work with, although it doesn’t guarantee that every word will be editable.

If you can only select the whole page as an image, the document may be a scan. A photograph of a printed sentence contains visible letters, but those letters aren’t necessarily stored as editable text.
There’s another possibility: the lettering was converted into shapes when the PDF was created. It can look perfectly sharp while offering no text for an editor to replace.

Folio doesn’t include OCR, the process used to recognize words in scanned images. For an image-only document, you’ll need an appropriate OCR workflow or the original source file before attempting text replacement.
Choose the right tool for the change
Adding a note and correcting an existing sentence are different jobs.
Suppose a proposal says “Delivery: October 18,” and you need to change it to October 28. You want to select the existing date and replace it.
If you’re adding “Please confirm delivery” beneath that sentence, an added text box makes sense.
This distinction explains a common frustration: choosing
Add Text
, clicking an existing paragraph, and expecting its words to become editable. That tool creates another text element.
For corrections, look for the control that edits original text. For comments, answers in blank spaces, or extra instructions, use added text.
How to edit text in a PDF file, step by step
1. Keep an untouched copy
Save a duplicate before making changes. A filename such as
proposal-original.pdf
makes it easy to distinguish the source from your edited version.
This is especially useful when correcting several details. If something shifts or a replacement looks wrong, you can compare the two documents instead of relying on memory.
For a first attempt, choose one short correction: a typo, a date, or a phone number.
2. Open the document and select Edit Text
Open the PDF in Folio’s editor, then choose
Edit Text
to access supported original text blocks.
The site currently states that editing and downloading these changes are free, with no Folio watermark added. You can also begin as a guest without signing in. Those details are listed on the
PDF editor page

Click the words you want to change. If the editor selects a larger block, read the whole selection before replacing anything. A line that looks like one sentence may be divided into several objects inside the file.
3. Make the smallest useful change
Replace the incorrect words while keeping the surrounding content intact.

For example, changing “Send the signed copy by Monday” to “Send the signed copy by Friday” is a fairly contained edit. Replacing it with a long paragraph of delivery instructions needs much more space.
After each correction, check its immediate surroundings. Does the sentence still fit? Has it moved close to a border? Does it overlap the next line?
Working through small changes makes problems easier to spot and undo.
4. Check the font and spacing
A replacement can be spelled correctly and still look out of place.

Start with the symptom you can observe
What happens
What it may mean
Useful next check
The page opens, but words cannot be selected
The wording may be part of a scan or outlined artwork.
Ask for the source file; check whether a separate OCR workflow is needed.
Words copy successfully, but the visible letters do not change
A searchable text layer may sit behind a page image, or the objects may be unsupported.

The best free PDF editor for this job should make that distinction clear. Adding a new text box is useful, but correcting words already on the page requires an original-text editing tool.
This guide explains how to make those changes with Folio, the editor at
thebestfreepdf.com
, and how to handle the formatting issues that can come with them.
Choose the right tool for the change
Before opening your file, decide what you need to accomplish:
Change an existing word or sentence:
Use original-text editing.
Put a name, answer, or note in an empty area:
Use Add Text.
Suggest a correction for someone else:
Use an annotation or highlight.

Suppose your flyer says “Thursday, October 15,” and the event moves to Friday. Adding “Friday, October 16” elsewhere leaves the incorrect date in place. Original-text editing lets you change the existing date where readers expect to find it.
Covering the old wording with a white rectangle can also leave the underlying text in the file. It may look corrected without actually replacing the content.

free PDF editor
includes both
Add Text
and
Edit Text
, with free downloads for supported original-text changes.
Check whether your PDF contains editable text
Try selecting a few words in your PDF viewer and copying them into a blank document. Readable pasted text is a useful clue that the file contains text an editor may recognize.
It isn’t a guarantee. Some PDFs contain complicated text structures, while scanned documents can have an invisible searchable text layer over a page image.

If you cannot select individual words, the page may be a scan, photograph, or artwork with letters converted into shapes. A scan needs optical character recognition, or OCR, before its words can be recognized as text. Searchable OCR output does not necessarily make the visible page directly editable.
Folio currently does not include OCR. Its
PDF text editor
supports compatible text blocks, with a limit of 10 MB and 100 pages for original-text editing. Replacement text currently supports Latin characters.
If your document falls outside those requirements, getting the source file may save considerable effort.

1. Keep an untouched copy
Save a copy of the original before making changes. Give the working version a clear name, such as
community-flyer-revised.pdf

This makes comparisons easier and prevents confusion when several versions sit in your Downloads folder. For documents with repeated information, jot down every location that needs attention: the event date might appear in the heading, schedule, and registration instructions.
2. Open the PDF and select Edit Text
Go to
thebestfreepdf.com/edit-pdf
and choose your PDF or drag it into the upload area.
Once the document opens, navigate to the correct page and select
Edit Text
. Click a supported text block and type your correction directly on the page. Use this control when replacing existing wording;
Add Text
creates a separate addition.
Start with one small correction. It gives you a chance to see how the document responds before working through the whole file.
3. Replace the wording carefully
Change only what needs changing, and reread the complete sentence afterward.
For the flyer example, replacing “Thursday” with “Friday” is only part of the job. You also need to update the date and check whether another paragraph still mentions Thursday.
Keep replacement wording close to the original length when possible. Changing “Room 4” to “Room 7” usually requires less space than changing it to “Conference Room, Second Floor.”
If the longer wording is necessary, check the surrounding layout immediately. Correct information is not useful if it runs into another line or disappears beyond a text block.
4. Match the surrounding formatting
Check the replacement’s font, size, and color against nearby text. Look at spacing as well: a word can use a similar-looking font and still occupy noticeably more room.

original-text editing page
Avoid shrinking a whole paragraph just to squeeze in one extra phrase. Shorter wording or a revision in the source document may produce a cleaner result.

Preview the changed page, then choose
Download PDF
Open the downloaded file and review it independently of the editor. Check:
The spelling, dates, names, and numbers you changed.
Line breaks and spacing around each correction.
Any text close to borders, images, or page edges.
Repeated details elsewhere in the document.

Consider a two-column newsletter. Adding three sentences to the left column may require moving several paragraphs, adjusting an image, and continuing text on another page. A small wording change has become a layout revision.

Use direct PDF editing for focused corrections: a misspelled name, an outdated room number, or a short instruction. If you need to rewrite sections or reorganize the document, edit the source file and export a fresh PDF when possible.
That choice can save more time than trying to repair each crowded text block individually.

The main editor uploads your PDF and saves the workspace in private cloud storage. Guest workspaces expire after 24 hours; signing in lets you retain files in your account. Original-text processing also sends the document to Folio. These details appear in the site’s
privacy policy
Download the finished version somewhere you can find it again. A saved editing session and the PDF you intend to send are separate things.
Make the correction, then check the whole sentence

after.author: Folio editorial

content.text: A new venue name appears on the cover, agenda, and contact page. Editing the first occurrence leaves the others wrong. Find and replace can help when the same correction belongs in several places, but the search must be specific and every replacement still needs review.
This workflow uses
Folio’s dedicated PDF text editor

and its Find & replace panel. It updates matching wording inside supported editable text blocks across the document. It does not search the meaning of sentences, recognize words inside a scan, or automatically reflow the layout.
Decide whether every occurrence should change

First write down the old value, its replacement, and where you expect it to appear. For a fictional workshop pack, the change might be “Room 4” to “Room 7” on three pages. Check whether a historical note or an example should still mention the old room. If different occurrences need different treatment, edit their blocks individually.

Choose the longest useful search phrase that still matches each intended location. Searching for the digit “4” could also change page references, times, and telephone numbers. Searching for “Room 4” is more specific, but can still match the beginning of “Room 40.” Specific wording reduces accidental matches; it does not remove the need to inspect them.
Find
Replace with
What to check
Room 4
Room 7
Check longer labels such as Room 40, which contain the same substring.
15 October 2026
22 October 2026
Numeric dates such as 15/10/2026 will need a separate review.
North Studio
North Design Studio
Check narrow headers and cells because the replacement is longer.
draft
final
Review sentences and filenames; the intended meaning may differ by location.
Run a controlled replacement
Keep the original PDF and open a working copy in the dedicated text editor.
Choose Upload for text editing to inspect supported blocks. The processor accepts up to 10 MB and 100 pages.
Open Find & replace. Enter the original phrase in Find and the new wording in Replace with.
Choose whether Match case should be enabled, then select Replace across document.
Read the replacement count. If it differs from your expected count, investigate before downloading.
Choose Update PDF preview and visit every affected page to check wording and placement.
Download PDF, open the saved file in a separate reader, and verify the changes there.

Use Undo text change if a replacement touched unintended text. Then refine the search or make individual corrections. The displayed replacement count counts matches in editable blocks; it is not a count of changed pages and is not proof that every visible occurrence has been corrected.
Understand exactly what matching does

The Find input is literal text. Characters such as a period or parentheses are searched as characters, not as regular-expression instructions. Match case distinguishes uppercase and lowercase when enabled. With it disabled, matching ignores case, but the replacement is inserted exactly as you typed it; it does not adapt to each occurrence’s capitalization.

Matching is not restricted to whole words. For example, searching for “art” can also match that sequence inside “start.” Use a fuller phrase or edit the individual block when a short word has several uses. Check both headings and body text if their capitalization should differ.

The operation searches the current wording of supported text blocks, including edits you have already made in the workspace. A second replacement therefore works on the result of the first. Plan the order and avoid running the same action repeatedly without checking what remains.
Why a visible phrase can produce no match

A sentence may be split between text blocks even when it looks continuous. Find and replace does not join separate blocks to match a phrase. Select the relevant blocks and inspect their wording; a shorter search may locate a fragment, but confirm that it will not affect unrelated passages.

A printed date may use a different separator, a different spelling, or a line break. An occurrence on a scanned appendix may be pixels rather than supported text. Do not shorten a search down to a single common digit just to make the counter increase. Review alternate spellings and image-only locations separately.
For a PDF that has no usable blocks, the
guide to text that will not edit
explains how to distinguish scans, searchable image layers, and unsupported objects. Folio does not include OCR.
Review the layout as well as the wording

A repeated phrase can sit in a wide paragraph on one page and a narrow table cell on another. Replacing “North Studio” with “North Design Studio” may fit the paragraph but collide with the amount column. Visit every affected location, including headers and footers, before treating the change as finished.

The editor does not automatically reflow paragraphs. Replacement text currently supports Latin characters, and a missing character in the original font may require substitution. Inspect the preview at normal reading size and compare alignment, line endings, and nearby content. If several locations need rebuilding, revising the source document is usually easier.
Verify the actual file you will share
Search the downloaded PDF for the old phrase and inspect any remaining matches.
Search for the new phrase and compare its locations with your expected list.
Visually review scanned pages and alternate spellings that text search may miss.
Check the new wording, page count, and layout in an independent reader.
Use a recognizable revised filename and attach that exact download.

Text search is a consistency check, not a redaction check. Changing a visible name does not prove all personal information has been removed from the PDF. Keep the original privately and use a separate redaction workflow when permanent removal is required.
Understand the upload before starting

The dedicated text editor previews your file locally before Upload for text editing. Inspection and text processing send the document to Folio. Opening it in the main PDF editor uses a separate private cloud-saving workflow. The
privacy page
describes those differences. A downloaded PDF is your separate finished copy; keep it before closing the working tab.

before.author: Folio Editorial

content.text: A translated PDF should help someone use the document, not simply replace its words. Headings must still guide the reader, labels must still belong to the right diagrams, and dates or reference numbers must remain easy to verify. Preparing the source and reviewing the result are both part of that work.

Folio provides a translation workspace where you can choose languages and compare original and translated pages. Processing depends on a connected translation service. The workflow below explains how to prepare your document and what to check when translation is available.
Check the workspace’s service status first. If it shows Service not connected, you can preview the original PDF, but translation processing is not currently available.
Begin with the clearest source PDF

Use the document exported from its original authoring application when you have it. Clear text and a straightforward layout give you a better starting point than a low-quality photograph of a printed page. Check that the PDF opens normally and that every page is present before translating it.

If you only have a scan, inspect its orientation, contrast, and readability. A skewed or faint page is harder to review in either language. Recognition of scanned content depends on the connected document service and source quality; Folio does not provide a separate OCR tool in this workflow.

The current translation workspace accepts PDFs up to 10 MB and 20 pages. For a longer document, use Split PDF to prepare clearly named sections. Keep related paragraphs, tables, and their explanatory notes together where possible, then maintain a simple list of the sections you have translated and reviewed.
Choose the source and target languages deliberately

Original language controls how the source is interpreted. You can use Auto-detect or choose a supported language explicitly. If you already know the language, selecting it makes your intended source clear. Translate into sets the output language, and it must differ from the selected source.

A document containing several languages deserves extra attention. A title, a quoted passage, and the main body may not all need the same treatment. Review the original first and note anything that should remain unchanged, such as a product name, an address, or an identifier. Do not assume a language selection will resolve every mixed-language passage correctly.
Translate and compare the result
Open Translate PDF and confirm that processing is available.
Choose your PDF and inspect the original page preview.
Set Original language and Translate into, then start translation.
Wait for the translated result and review the corresponding pages alongside the original. On a smaller screen, switch between the original and translation views.
Check every page before downloading. Translation downloads are free when the processing service is available.

Take a short document as an example: a three-page event guide with a schedule, a venue description, and arrival instructions. Confirm the schedule’s times and dates against the original, review the venue name and address, and read the arrival steps as a complete sequence. A sentence can sound natural while still changing a detail that matters.
Review meaning before polishing appearance
Check names, reference numbers, dates, units, and numerical values against the original.
Look for repeated terms and confirm that the same concept is expressed consistently.
Read instructions in order and check whether the intended action is still clear.
Review headings and table labels together with the content they describe.
Ask a fluent reviewer to resolve wording you cannot confidently evaluate yourself.

Automatic translation can provide a useful draft, but it should not be treated as an assurance of accuracy. For material where a misunderstanding would have serious consequences, arrange an appropriate qualified review before relying on or distributing the translation. The tool does not provide a certified translation service.
Check layout after the language changes

Translated text can take more or less space than the original. Watch for lines running into neighboring content, headings wrapping awkwardly, and table cells becoming crowded. Compare the positions of labels, captions, and footnotes rather than checking only the main paragraphs.

Fonts and text direction may also affect the appearance. Review the translated pages at a readable zoom level and inspect the exported file again before sharing it. Folio offers separate original and translated views; the current workflow does not create a bilingual PDF with both versions combined.
Keep the original and identify the translated copy

Use a filename that includes the target language, such as event-guide-spanish.pdf, and keep the source separately. This makes later corrections easier to trace and helps the recipient identify the version they received. If the source changes, compare the affected sections before reusing an older translation.

or
Rotate PDF
where needed, then visit
Translate PDF
to check availability and begin your review workflow.

before.title: PDF Conversion Guide: Choose the Right Format for Your Next Task
before.author: Folio Editorial

content.text: “Convert this PDF” can mean several different things. You might need a slide image, a collection of receipts in one document, editable words for your notes, or an Office file for further work. Choosing the output format first prevents unnecessary conversions and makes the result easier to evaluate.

A PDF is designed around pages. When you convert it, some of the information that matters on a page may no longer behave the same way. Images preserve the visible appearance, plain text keeps the words, and editable document formats attempt to reconstruct a working layout.

Export PDF pages as JPG or PNG

Use PDF to JPG for page previews where a compact image is helpful. PNG is a useful alternative for diagrams, fine lines, and text-heavy pages because its image encoding avoids lossy compression artifacts. The selected resolution still determines how much detail the rendered page contains.
Open PDF to JPG or PDF to PNG and choose your PDF.
Select the pages you need. Leave the range empty for all pages, or enter a selection such as 1-3, 6.
Choose an image resolution appropriate to where you will use the result.
Run the conversion and download the ZIP archive containing one image per selected page.
Open an exported image at its intended display size and check the smallest important text.

An exported page image no longer contains selectable PDF text or interactive fields. A visible link becomes part of the picture rather than a clickable PDF link. Keep the original PDF if recipients need to search, copy text, or interact with a form.
Turn images into a single PDF

Image to PDF is useful for grouping receipt photos, sketches, and existing JPG or PNG exports. Add the images, arrange their order, and choose fitted pages or A4. Each image becomes its own PDF page. A4 places the image on a portrait sheet with margins; fitted pages follow the image proportions.

Prepare the images before combining them. Rotate a sideways photo, remove an accidental duplicate, and check that handwriting is readable. Folio currently accepts JPG and PNG in this tool, with up to 20 images per batch. Convert other formats, such as HEIC, before adding them.

Creating a PDF from a photograph does not recognize the words inside it. The resulting document contains page images. If searchable text is essential, you will need a separate OCR workflow; Folio does not currently offer standalone OCR.
Extract words for notes and reuse

PDF to text extracts existing selectable text and downloads it as a plain text file. It is a practical choice when you want the wording from a report without its typography, page furniture, or images. Select only the pages you need to keep the output focused.

Read the extracted text before reusing it. Multi-column pages can produce an unexpected reading order, and tables may lose the visual relationship between cells. Plain text does not preserve fonts, images, or complex layout. If the PDF is an image-only scan, there may be no selectable words to extract.
Understand Office conversion availability

Folio also has workspaces for PDF to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. These conversions depend on a connected conversion service. Check the tool’s availability message before planning your workflow. If it displays Service not connected, processing is unavailable; that message does not mean your PDF is damaged.

When the service is available, open the converted file in the target application and review it there. Check paragraph flow in Word, rows and columns in Excel, and object placement in PowerPoint. Converting a finished page back into editable objects can change its layout, so leave time for a final adjustment pass.
Convert once, review, then share

Work from the best available original and avoid unnecessary round trips between formats. Give the output a descriptive name that identifies its purpose, such as workshop-page-03.png or receipts-march.pdf. Keep the source until you have confirmed that the converted copy does everything the recipient needs.
